text: Hypothesis evaluation: Q mechanism design -> P contract implementability. Q provides revelation principle + nested cyclical monotonicity for settings with unknown capabilities + sandbagging. P studies self-negotiated contracts in CT game but does not model capability uncertainty. Concrete result: characterize which P-contracts are implementable when agents can conceal capabilities. Key insight: Q one-sided imitation (capabilities concealable but not counterfeitable) maps to contract bargaining where agents may understate abilities. Prediction: formal contracts more robust to sandbagging than natural contracts because compilation constrains strategic misrepresentation. Objection: Q assumes principal-designer; P has peer negotiation. Need to adapt Q tools to decentralized setting or show principal-agent framing emerges.

Q provides mechanism design tools for unknown capabilities/alignment: revelation principle, nested cyclical monotonicity, one-sided imitation (can conceal but not counterfeit capabilities). P studies contract negotiation in CT game but lacks theoretical framework for implementability under capability uncertainty. The connexion is supported: Q explicitly models sandbagging; P contracts could fail if agents misrepresent capabilities during negotiation. However, P abstract does not indicate whether capability misrepresentation was observed or controlled for - this is a key gap to verify.

Sharpened hypothesis: Q nested cyclical monotonicity characterizes implementable P-contracts under capability uncertainty. Concrete result: A contract in P is implementable iff it satisfies nested cyclical monotonicity w.r.t. agent capability types. Non-obvious insight: formal contracts satisfy this condition more readily than natural contracts because compilation removes ambiguity that enables sandbagging. Testable prediction: when agents can conceal capabilities, formal contracts maintain cooperation gains while natural contracts degrade. Support: Q Thm 1 (revelation principle) + Q sandbagging analysis map to P contract space. Gap: Q assumes principal-designer; P has symmetric negotiation. Resolution: model negotiation as alternating principal-designer rounds or show symmetric mechanism inherits implementability conditions.

Sharpened hypothesis: Qs one-sided imitation (conceal but not counterfeit capabilities) predicts differential vulnerability of Ps contract types. Formal contracts (compile to code) may require precise capability claims during negotiation - vulnerable to sandbagging if agents understate capabilities to get easier terms. Natural contracts (reinterpretation allowed) may be less vulnerable because vagueness doesnt require precise capability revelation. Testable: re-analyze P negotiation transcripts for capability claims; check if formal contracts show more evidence of strategic understatement. Qs nested cyclical monotonicity characterizes which contract menus are implementable despite this.

Unresolved issues for publication claim: (1) Structural mismatch: Q mechanism design assumes principal designing for agents; P has peer-to-peer negotiation. Need to show Q tools apply to symmetric setting or that asymmetry emerges endogenously. (2) Mathematical mapping: nested cyclical monotonicity defined over allocation rules; P contracts are bargaining outcomes. Need explicit mapping between Q allocation space and P contract space. (3) Empirical support: abstract scan claims P provides experimental platform, but P abstract only states contracts improve cooperation, not that capability uncertainty was tested. May need new experiments. (4) Novelty threshold: Is this Q-theory-applied-to-P or does it generate new theory? The formal-vs-natural explanation via sandbagging-robustness could be the novel contribution.

Path forward: (1) Formalize P contract space as mechanism design problem - show negotiation induces implicit allocation rule over capability types. (2) Apply Q nested cyclical monotonicity to derive implementability conditions. (3) Prove formal contracts satisfy conditions more robustly than natural contracts under sandbagging. (4) Empirical test: re-analyze P data stratifying by capability uncertainty or run new CT experiments with hidden capability treatments. Publication claim stands if steps 1-3 yield theorem + step 4 supports prediction. If structural mismatch in (1) cannot be resolved, hypothesis fails.

Three objections to consider: (1) P reports contracts improve cooperation - if sandbagging were prevalent, would this hold? Either LLMs dont sandbag strategically in this setup, or the experimental design controls for it. Need to verify. (2) Q assumes a principal designing mechanisms; P studies peer negotiation between agents. The mapping isnt direct - whos the mechanism designer in P? May need to reinterpret Qs framework for decentralized settings. (3) Gain=55 suggests modest contribution - this extends rather than transforms either paper. Might work as a theoretical companion to P, but standalone publication would need stronger novelty.

Direct reading of Q abstract confirms: (1) one-sided imitation structure where capabilities can be concealed but not counterfeited; (2) revelation principle + nested cyclical monotonicity characterize implementable policies; (3) sandbagging is explicit application (more capable agent pretends less capable). Q is theoretical mechanism design framework for unknown capabilities/alignment.

Direct reading of P abstract confirms: (1) Studies self-negotiated contracts in CT game (bargaining + navigation); (2) Compares formal contracts (compile to code) vs natural contracts (reinterpretation allowed); (3) Finds contracts improve cooperative outcomes; (4) No mention of capability uncertainty, sandbagging, or mechanism design framework. P is experimental study of contract-based cooperation with LLM agents.

Critical structural mismatch verified: Q assumes principal-designer setting (principal designs mechanism for agents), but P has peer-to-peer negotiation between agents with no external principal. In P, agents are both mechanism designers AND participants simultaneously. This is not a minor gap - Qs revelation principle and nested cyclical monotonicity are proven for principal-agent settings. Applying to P requires either: (a) showing P negotiation induces equivalent principal-agent structure, or (b) extending Q theory to decentralized symmetric settings. Neither is trivial.

Q abstract confirms: mechanism design for unknown capabilities/alignment with one-sided imitation (conceal but not counterfeit). Nested cyclical monotonicity characterizes implementable policies. Sandbagging is explicit application. P abstract confirms: self-negotiated contracts in CT game, formal vs natural contracts, improves cooperation. BUT P abstract does not mention capability uncertainty, hidden types, or mechanism design framing. P treats contracts as commitment devices for temporal cooperation problems, not as mechanisms for eliciting capability information. Key gap: Ps agents negotiate contracts to solve commitment problems (early cost, late benefit), not to reveal private capability information.
